claims.text: The initial material is a dendritic, single-phase BCC TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy.
Introducing oxygen during spark plasma sintering can induce TiO precipitation in the BCC alloy.
An oxygen-triggered post-sintering heat treatment can induce TiO precipitation.
The oxygen intervention will produce fine TiO particles.
The TiO precipitates will be dispersed within the BCC matrix.
The TiO precipitates will also be distributed along grain boundaries.
TiO precipitates strengthen the alloy by pinning dislocations.
TiO precipitates stabilize a fine-grained microstructure against high-temperature recovery.
A fine-grained BCC matrix can contribute grain-boundary strengthening.
The proposed precipitate and grain-boundary mechanisms will improve yield-strength retention at elevated temperature.
The baseline TiVNbTa alloy has a yield strength of approximately 330 MPa at 1273 K.
At 1273 K, the oxygen-modified TiVNbTa alloy will have a significantly higher yield strength than the approximately 330 MPa baseline.
The modified alloy may approach strengths achieved by precipitation-strengthened refractory alloys.
Testing should be conducted at approximately 1273 K under mechanical loading relevant to a W–CuCrZr intermediate layer and in an inert or controlled atmosphere.
The strength increment and optimal oxygen level will depend on processing parameters and precipitate distribution.

The hypothesis can be tested by comparing oxygen-modified and nominally oxygen-free TiVNbTa controls under identical mechanical testing at 1273 K while measuring precipitates, grain size, dislocation density, and strength.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant yield-strength improvement at 1273 K, or failure to form the anticipated fine, well-distributed TiO precipitates, is defined as falsification.
